title: Coherence as Thermodynamic Organization: Toward a Non-Equilibrium Turbulence Theory
authors: Sharath S. Girimaji
abstract: Since the foundational studies in the late nineteenth century, fluid turbulence has stood as a profound, unsolved challenge in classical physics. Much of this enduring difficulty stems from non-equilibrium turbulence, where the lack of a unifying physical framework for macroscopic coherent structures has hampered predictive flow modeling. Here, we establish a foundational bridge between non-equilibrium statistical physics and turbulent coherent structures through the renormalized Navier-Stokes equations. We demonstrate that all forms of turbulent coherence are fundamentally universal thermodynamic responses mandated by macroscopic energy throughput imbalances. Depending on topological access to bifurcations, these formations manifest either as transient adjustments (analogous to Kubo's near-equilibrium fluctuations) or as autonomous, transformative states (mirroring Prigogine's far-from-equilibrium dissipative structures). By introducing a computable, effective thermodynamic order parameter ($Π$), this paradigm establishes a rigorous foundation for non-equilibrium theory, enabling unequivocal identification of necessary flow resolution in continuously driven, dissipative continuum systems.

infographic.key_insight: Turbulent coherent structures are framed as universal thermodynamic responses to macroscopic energy throughput imbalance, captured by a computable effective order parameter (Π).
infographic.engineering_relevance: This could give engineers a principled way to identify when a flow needs finer resolution and to distinguish transient fluctuations from self-sustaining coherent structures in non-equilibrium turbulence.
method: Use renormalized Navier–Stokes equations to connect turbulence to non-equilibrium statistical physics.
Define an effective thermodynamic order parameter (Π) for coherent-structure detection.
Classify coherence by whether the flow response is a transient adjustment or an autonomous dissipative state.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a theoretical framework and claims a computable parameter for identifying necessary flow resolution, but it does not report specific datasets or numerical validation results.
infographic.watch_item: The proposal is highly conceptual, so practical adoption will depend on how Π is computed and validated across diverse turbulent flows.
infographic.paper_title: Coherence as Thermodynamic Organization: Toward a Non-Equilibrium Turbulence Theory

title: NeuroForge: A Self-Correcting, Geometry-Native Neural CFD Engine with Calibrated Physics-Residual Trust
authors: Ali Jabbary, Kasra Ghanavati
abstract: Machine-learning surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) predict steady flow fields orders of magnitude faster than classical solvers, but emit a single field with no built-in way to know whether to trust it -- especially out of distribution. We close the loop with the governing physics: we compute the discretised steady-RANS residual of the prediction and ask what jobs it can do. Our central finding is a two-way dissociation: the physics residual is a reliable, backbone-robust trust signal (it tells you where the prediction is wrong) but a poor correction objective (it does not tell you how to fix it). As a trust signal, the residual's per-case rank correlation with field error is consistently positive across three architecturally distinct backbones (Transolver 0.625+-0.019; grid Geo-FNO ~0.40, lifted to 0.83 by a learned corrector; MeshGraphNet 0.851+-0.058) and generalizes to a second dataset and flow regime (DeepCFD laminar bluff bodies, rho=0.77+-0.12). A split-conformal layer attains target coverage (0.902+-0.008 at the 0.90 target) and, paired with a deep-ensemble sigma, yields an input-adaptive band (ECE 0.074). As a correction objective or acceptance gate the residual fails: iteration sweeps raise the PDE residual while lowering field error. Alongside the trust layer we deploy a supervised deep-equilibrium corrector trained toward ground truth that reduces volume-field MSE on all three seeds (mse_u -9%, mse_v -21%, mse_p -25%) on the SOTA backbone; a controlled ablation zeroing the corrector's residual input matches it, so the gain is attributable to the learned correction, not residual-conditioning. We report caveats plainly: correction quality is backbone-dependent, and the coverage guarantee holds under exchangeability. The contribution is a self-auditing trust layer, the residual's two roles, and the learned self-correction it accompanies.

infographic.key_insight: Physics residuals are good at telling you when a CFD surrogate is wrong, but not at telling you how to correct it.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables fast surrogate CFD with an added self-auditing trust layer and a learned corrector for safer deployment on new flow cases.
method: Compute the discretized steady-RANS residual of surrogate predictions.
Use residuals for calibrated trust via split conformal prediction and deep-ensemble uncertainty.
Train a supervised deep-equilibrium corrector toward ground truth for self-correction.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three backbones and a second dataset, residual-error rank correlation stays positive (e.g., Transolver 0.625±0.019, MeshGraphNet 0.851±0.058), while conformal coverage hits 0.902±0.008 at a 0.90 target.
infographic.watch_item: The correction benefit is backbone-dependent, and the coverage guarantee only holds under exchangeability.
infographic.paper_title: NeuroForge: A Self-Correcting, Geometry-Native Neural CFD Engine with Calibrated Physics-Residual Trust

title: Gradient-free learning of a closed-loop wall controller for turbulent drag reduction
authors: Giorgio Maria Cavallazzi, Miguel Pérez Cuadrado, Alfredo Pinelli
abstract: Closed-loop wall control learnt by multi-agent reinforcement learning can lower skin-friction drag in turbulent channels, but these gradient-based policies are trained on small periodic boxes and exhibit reduced performance when carried over to a larger domain. We recently showed that such policies are also prone to saturated bang-bang actuations that collapse into standing streamwise waves whose scale is set by the computational box rather than by the near-wall cycle, and proposed architectural fixes that avoid these degeneracies. Here, we employ Evolution Strategy (ES) to optimise a recurrent closed-loop controller directly on a large turbulent channel at $\mathit{Re}_τ\simeq180$, evaluating policy performance over full flow episodes using an energy-aware criterion and processing candidate policies in parallel. To our knowledge, this is the first application of an evolution strategy to the control of a turbulent flow. The ES controller reduces the skin friction by about $26\%$, exceeding the gradient-based multi-agent controller of Cavallazzi et al. (2026), GRU-MARL, trained on a minimal box ($17\%$), and marginally exceeding classic opposition control (OC, $22\%$). A wall-normal decomposition of the friction, Reynolds-stress profiles and anisotropy invariants show that the ES and opposition-controlled flows follow separate trajectories through the buffer layer, reaching comparable drag reduction by different reorganisations of the near-wall turbulence. In particular, the ES actuation correlates predominantly with the streamwise velocity fluctuations rather than with the wall-normal velocity that classical OC targets.

infographic.key_insight: Evolution Strategy can train a recurrent closed-loop wall controller directly on a large turbulent channel and achieve stronger drag reduction than prior small-box gradient-based policies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a more robust route to deployable active flow control for skin-friction reduction in turbulent channels, with better transfer to realistic domain sizes.
method: Optimize a recurrent policy with Evolution Strategy instead of gradients.
Evaluate candidate controllers on full turbulent-flow episodes using an energy-aware objective.
Train and test directly in a large channel at Re_τ ≈ 180, avoiding small-box dependence.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the large-domain channel, the ES controller reduced skin-friction drag by about 26%, compared with 17% for GRU-MARL on a minimal box and 22% for classic opposition control.
infographic.watch_item: Despite the performance gain, the controller design still needs careful validation for robustness, cost of parallel evaluations, and generalization to other Reynolds numbers or geometries.
infographic.paper_title: Gradient-free learning of a closed-loop wall controller for turbulent drag reduction

title: A multi-scale feature enhanced graph neural network for fluid dynamics prediction in complex geometries
authors: Li Xiao, Tianyu Li, Yiye Zou, Mingjie Zhang, Xiaogangd Deng
abstract: Industrial design in fields such as vehicle and aerospace engineering often relies on large-scale numerical simulations to evaluate fluid dynamics performance, which can incur substantial computational costs. Deep neural networks have shown promise in improving simulation efficiency, especially graph neural networks (GNNs), which demonstrate great potential due to their flexibility with unstructured data. However, GNNs face challenges when dealing with tasks involving complex geometries and large-scale meshes. In this paper, we propose the Multi-scale Feature Enhanced Graph Neural Network (ME-GNN) to tackle these challenges. ME-GNN employs a graph neural network with a two-step message-passing mechanism to capture detailed local features effectively. Additionally, it integrates an Attention U-Net with uniform grid discretization, enabling the extraction of both fine and coarse features. The model also utilizes K-hop sampling to construct subgraphs, facilitating efficient training on large datasets while preserving detailed local features. We evaluated ME-GNN on three benchmark datasets and achieved state-of-the-art results: a relative L2 error of 0.0196 for the velocity field and 0.0556 for the surface pressure on ShapeNet-Car, a normalized mean squared error of 0.0033 for the flow field on AirfRANS, and a relative L2 error of 0.1416 for the surface pressure on DrivAerNet.

infographic.key_insight: ME-GNN improves fluid prediction in complex geometries by combining local graph message passing with multi-scale feature extraction from grid-based attention U-Net features.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method targets faster, more accurate surrogate modeling for expensive CFD workflows in automotive and aerospace design on large, irregular meshes.
method: Two-step GNN message passing to capture detailed local flow interactions.
Attention U-Net on uniform grids to extract both fine and coarse spatial features.
K-hop subgraph sampling for scalable training on large meshes while preserving locality.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model reports strong benchmark performance across ShapeNet-Car, AirfRANS, and DrivAerNet, including relative L2 errors of 0.0196 for velocity and 0.0556 for surface pressure on ShapeNet-Car.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on careful subgraph sampling and grid/mesh alignment, which can be challenging for very large or highly irregular geometries.
infographic.paper_title: A multi-scale feature enhanced graph neural network for fluid dynamics prediction in complex geometries

title: Mixing and sharpening at the interface of a two-layer fluid forced by random jets
authors: Noé Clavier, Hugo Pradel, Romain Volk, Mickaël Bourgoin, Yvan Dossmann
abstract: Understanding mixing at density interfaces is essential for predicting transport in stratified environmental flows. Laboratory studies have mostly relied on steady, spatially uniform forcing, whereas turbulence in nature is intermittent and heterogeneous. Here, we present experiments on a two-layer salt-stratified fluid forced by random turbulent bursts generated with a randomly actuated synthetic jet array (RASJA). Density fields are recorded with the light attenuation technique, allowing us to resolve the interface evolution. We measure that the upward velocity of the interface decreases with the density jump, in agreement with the power-law found in previous oscillating-grid studies. At large density differences, the interface sharpens during mixing, contrary to the smaller density jump case. Background potential energy analysis demonstrates irreversible mixing in both cases, with comparable energy changes. These results extend classical laboratory observations to a more isotropic forcing, offering new insights into the dynamics of mixing in geophysical settings.

infographic.key_insight: Random, intermittent jet forcing can mix a two-layer stratified fluid while the interface may either sharpen or rise more slowly depending on the density jump.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results inform how turbulent bursts in natural and industrial stratified flows can alter transport, entrainment, and interface stability.
method: Two-layer salt-stratified fluid experiments forced by a randomly actuated synthetic jet array (RASJA).
Interface evolution measured with light attenuation imaging.
Background potential energy used to quantify irreversible mixing and compare cases.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that interface rise velocity decreases with density jump and that mixing remains irreversible in both regimes, with comparable energy changes.
infographic.watch_item: These findings come from laboratory conditions and a specific forcing setup, so scaling them to fully natural flows or different stratifications should be done cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: Mixing and sharpening at the interface of a two-layer fluid forced by random jets

title: Numerical Simulation of Turbulent Concentric Annular Pipe Flow using One-Dimensional Turbulence (ODT): Part 2: Heat Transfer
authors: Pei-Yun Tsai, Heiko Schmidt, Marten Klein
abstract: Turbulent concentric coaxial (annular) pipe flow with passive heat transfer is theoretically analyzed and numerically modeled in an extended parametric range using the stochastic one-dimensional turbulence (ODT) model. ODT provides predictive capabilities by fully resolving viscous, conductive, and turbulent advective transport processes along a representative radial coordinate within a dimensionally reduced and stochastic model formulation. Using a fixed model calibration for moderate and low Prandtl numbers, $Pr=0.71$ and $0.025$, effects of radius ratio, $η=R_{\rm i}/R_{\rm o}$ are investigated up to a highly turbulent flow regime. The analytical expression of the inner wall boundary layer yields a logarithmic law of the wall for the passive temperature. These results suggest that a conventional linear expression is inadequate for representing near-wall low-order statistics in the radial gap, in particular at the cylindrical inner wall. Additionally, the log-law region falls short if curvature and finite Reynolds number effects are not considered. Analytical boundary layer profiles fitting numerical predictions form the basis for heat transfer scaling relations. Heat transfer scalings are parameterized by a Nusselt correlation, which is extended to account for radius ratio effects. The findings demonstrate that the radius ratio has a significant impact on the thermal statistics over the two curved walls and should be considered even at high Reynolds numbers and low Prandtl numbers.

infographic.key_insight: ODT predicts that in turbulent concentric annular pipe flow, curvature and radius ratio strongly reshape passive heat transfer, so the inner-wall temperature field is not well captured by a simple linear near-wall model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results support improved Nusselt correlations for annular thermal design, especially when wall curvature and finite Reynolds number effects matter even at low Prandtl number.
method: Stochastic one-dimensional turbulence (ODT) model with a dimensionally reduced radial coordinate
Fully resolves viscous, conductive, and turbulent advective transport
Calibrated for Pr=0.71 and 0.025 and extended across radius ratio and Reynolds number ranges
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical boundary-layer profiles matched against numerical ODT predictions and used to build radius-ratio-dependent heat-transfer scalings.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed correlations are tied to a fixed ODT calibration and may need revalidation outside the tested Prandtl, Reynolds, and geometry ranges.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical Simulation of Turbulent Concentric Annular Pipe Flow using One-Dimensional Turbulence (ODT): Part 2: Heat Transfer

title: Heuristic Learning for Active Flow Control Using Coding Agents
authors: Paul Garnier, Jonathan Viquerat, Elie Hachem
abstract: Active flow control involves nonlinear dynamics, partial observations, and computationally expensive simulations, making controller design particularly challenging. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has emerged as a powerful framework for such problems, but its success typically relies on large numbers of simulator interactions and produces neural-network policies whose decision process often remains difficult to interpret. In this work, we investigate a different paradigm: instead of optimizing neural-network parameters, we use modern coding agents to search directly for explicit executable feedback laws. We introduce a constrained heuristic-learning protocol in which an agent iteratively proposes, evaluates, and revises controller implementations while interacting exclusively through the public benchmark interface. The proposed framework is evaluated on 13 active flow-control benchmarks spanning one, two, and three-dimensional problems and compared against the strongest available DRL baselines under identical simulation budgets. The discovered heuristic controllers match or outperform the best DRL policy in 10 of the 13 environments while remaining compact, interpretable, and directly inspectable. Beyond aggregate performance, the resulting controllers reveal physically meaningful feedback mechanisms, transfer successfully across more challenging configurations, and remain competitive under varying Reynolds and Rayleigh numbers, actuator counts, and observation sparsity. These results suggest that heuristic learning through coding agents constitutes a credible and complementary alternative to conventional reinforcement learning, combining competitive performance with physically interpretable controller representations. Prompts and source code are available at https://github.com/DonsetPG/fluid-heuristic-learning.

infographic.key_insight: Coding agents can directly search for explicit, interpretable feedback laws for active flow control and achieve performance comparable to or better than DRL.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical alternative for flow-control engineering when simulation budgets are limited and controller interpretability matters.
method: Use a constrained heuristic-learning loop where an agent proposes controller code.
Evaluate each candidate only through the public benchmark simulator interface.
Iteratively revise the executable policy under fixed simulation budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 13 active flow-control benchmarks, the discovered heuristic controllers matched or outperformed the best DRL policy in 10 environments under identical simulation budgets.
infographic.watch_item: The approach still depends on iterative simulation-based evaluation, so scalability and robustness may vary with benchmark complexity and implementation quality.
infographic.paper_title: Heuristic Learning for Active Flow Control Using Coding Agents

title: Physics informed wavelet Fourier representation for multiscale fluid dynamics
authors: Chao Wang, Shilong Li, Yunpeng Wang, Tianbai Xiao, Zelong Yuan, Chenyue Xie
abstract: Multiscale fluid flows often contain localized flow structures, such as viscous shock layers, wet-dry fronts, steady viscous wakes, decaying vortical structures, and vortex-shedding patterns, whose accurate prediction requires the simultaneous preservation of global conservation trends and small-scale gradients. This study examines these flow-physics requirements through a physics-informed wavelet-Fourier (PIWF) representation for multiscale fluid dynamics. Instead of relying on a single monolithic neural approximator, the formulation separates two complementary components of the flow field within a physics-informed neural representation: long-range coherent modes through a Fourier-basis branch and localized steep-gradient or vortical features through a compactly supported wavelet branch. The outputs are fused with a residual multilayer perceptron using channel attention, and the governing equations, initial conditions, and boundary conditions are imposed directly through the physics-informed loss. The model is assessed on five canonical fluid-dynamics problems: Burgers' equation, the shallow water equations, Kovasznay flow, Taylor--Green vortex flow, and two-dimensional cylinder wake flow. The results show that PIWF improves the resolution of shock-like gradients, wet--dry interfaces, steady wake fields, decaying vortical structures, vorticity extrema, and broadband wake spectra relative to standard physics-informed neural networks and physics-informed Kolmogorov--Arnold networks. These findings indicate that a wavelet-Fourier physics-informed representation can provide a useful route for analyzing multiscale flow phenomena when high-fidelity interior reference data are limited or unavailable.

infographic.key_insight: PIWF splits multiscale fluid fields into global Fourier modes and localized wavelet features, then fuses them in a physics-informed network to better capture both smooth trends and sharp gradients.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical surrogate modeling strategy for CFD problems with shocks, fronts, wakes, and vortices when dense interior data are unavailable.
method: Fourier branch models long-range coherent flow structures.
Wavelet branch captures compact, localized steep-gradient and vortical features.
Residual MLP with channel attention fuses both branches under PDE, initial, and boundary constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on five canonical problems—Burgers, shallow water, Kovasznay flow, Taylor--Green vortex, and 2D cylinder wake—showing improved resolution of shocks, wet-dry fronts, wakes, vortices, and spectra versus PINNs and PI-KANs.
infographic.watch_item: The added branch fusion and attention may increase model complexity and tuning effort, so performance and stability should be checked carefully across new flow regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Physics informed wavelet Fourier representation for multiscale fluid dynamics

title: Emergent coordination and propulsion of a model spherical ciliate
authors: Hang Su, Timothy A Westwood, Eric E Keaveny
abstract: A longstanding challenge in biofluid dynamics research is a mechanistic understanding of the coordinated movement of motile cilia and its resulting ability to facilitate fluid transport. In this study, we develop numerical techniques to simultaneously compute the emergent coordination of and propulsion by filamentous model cilia covering the surface of a sphere. To accomplish this, we develop what we refer to as the filament oscillator model, in which each cilium has two dynamic degrees of freedom: a phase variable that maps to a specific shape in a prescribed sequence, and an angle that describes the overall orientation of the sequence. By varying a parameter related to cilium stiffness, we show that there is bistability between symplectic-like and diaplectic metachronal waves, provided that the stiffness is sufficiently low. Above the critical stiffness, only diaplectic waves emerge. Further, we analyse the propulsive capabilities and flow fields of the two emergent states, showing that diaplectic waves provide more efficient propulsion due to their shorter wavelengths. In addition, we examine how introducing beat-plane tilt leads to ciliate rotation while maintaining nearly identical emergent states and comparable swimming speeds.

infographic.key_insight: A spherical ciliate model with filament oscillators shows how local cilium stiffness can switch collective beating between symplectic-like and diaplectic metachronal waves, which in turn changes propulsion efficiency.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide design insight for synthetic cilia and active surface actuators, showing how tuning stiffness and beat geometry can control emergent coordination, swimming speed, and rotation.
method: Represent each cilium with two degrees of freedom: a phase along a prescribed beat sequence and an orientation angle.
Simulate cilia distributed over a sphere to compute emergent coordination and the resulting fluid-driven propulsion.
Vary cilium stiffness and beat-plane tilt to study transitions between wave states, flow fields, and rotation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical comparisons across stiffness values and beat-plane tilt, evaluating emergent wave type, propulsion efficiency, flow fields, and swimming speed.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions are based on a simplified filament oscillator model, so real ciliary geometry, compliance, and hydrodynamic coupling may shift the predicted wave transition threshold.
infographic.paper_title: Emergent coordination and propulsion of a model spherical ciliate

title: Feature-based manifold model of actuated wakes
authors: Alicia Rodríguez-Asensio, Guy Y. Cornejo Maceda, Bernd R. Noack, Stefano Discetti, Andrea Ianiro
abstract: We propose a feature-based reduced-order model to predict the transient dynamics of bluff-body wakes under arbitrary time-varying actuation. Starting point is a control-oriented POD Galerkin modeling which is challenged by incorporating time-varying actuations as a free input. Our model includes three key enablers. First, POD modes are replaced by a more accurate feature-based manifold of same dimension. Second, a state space is distilled from dynamic features which encapsulate time-varying coherent structures. Third, this state space is augmented for the transient actuation response. Thus, a simple analytical manifold dynamics is obtained. The approach is applied to the fluidic pinball at Re=30, a canonical configuration of three identical circular cylinders arranged in an equilateral triangle and immersed in uniform flow under symmetric actuation. The model is validated against several representative actuation scenarios and accurately reproduces the transient dynamics without requiring unsteady training data, providing an interpretable, observable-based and control-oriented framework. The proposed description of actuated bluff-body flows is expected to be generalisable to other configurations.

infographic.key_insight: The paper replaces POD modes with a feature-based manifold and augmented state space to predict transient bluff-body wake dynamics under arbitrary time-varying actuation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers an interpretable reduced-order surrogate for control-oriented flow prediction, useful for actuator design and real-time wake management in bluff-body systems.
method: Build a feature-based manifold with the same dimension as the original POD space
Distill the state from dynamic features that represent coherent structures over time
Augment the state space to capture transient response to time-varying actuation
infographic.evidence_signal: Validated on the fluidic pinball at Re=30 across several representative actuation scenarios, where it reproduces transient dynamics without unsteady training data.
infographic.watch_item: The model is demonstrated on a canonical low-Re configuration, so broader robustness and scaling to more complex flows still need verification.
infographic.paper_title: Feature-based manifold model of actuated wakes

title: Entropy-Constrained Machine Learning with Residual Data Augmentation for Modeling Chemical Kinetics
authors: Okezzi Ukorigho, Opeoluwa Owoyele
abstract: We present a physics-constrained machine learning framework for accelerating the direct numerical simulation (DNS) of turbulent reacting flows. The model replaces the direct evaluation of detailed chemical source terms with a surrogate that predicts reaction rates from a reduced thermochemical state. To improve physical consistency, the second law of thermodynamics is incorporated as a training constraint by enforcing non-negative entropy generation, which restricts the evolution of the thermochemical state to physically admissible directions and improves stability during time integration. The approach is demonstrated on DNS of a two-dimensional planar lean premixed methane-air flame interacting with a turbulent flow field. The model reproduces detailed-chemistry results with high fidelity while achieving more than an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost. Furthermore, a residual-based synthetic data augmentation strategy enables parametric exploration by constructing new training data from the original dataset, allowing accurate simulation at new inlet conditions without additional detailed-chemistry CFD runs. These results demonstrate that thermodynamically constrained machine learning can provide reliable and computationally efficient surrogates for detailed chemistry in high-fidelity combustion simulations.

infographic.key_insight: A thermodynamically constrained surrogate can replace expensive detailed chemical kinetics in DNS while preserving physical admissibility and accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables much faster turbulent combustion simulations with reliable predictions and lower computational cost, supporting design and analysis of reacting-flow systems.
method: Train a machine-learning model to predict reaction rates from a reduced thermochemical state instead of evaluating full chemistry.
Enforce the second law of thermodynamics by constraining entropy generation to be non-negative during training and time integration.
Use residual-based synthetic data augmentation to generate new training samples for unseen inlet conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a 2D lean premixed methane-air flame interacting with turbulence, the surrogate matches detailed-chemistry DNS with high fidelity and achieves more than an order-of-magnitude cost reduction.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on the quality of the reduced state, the entropy constraint formulation, and synthetic data assumptions, which may limit transferability outside the tested combustion regime.
infographic.paper_title: Entropy-Constrained Machine Learning with Residual Data Augmentation for Modeling Chemical Kinetics

title: Developing Machine Learning Models of Subgrid Turbulent Transport for Quiet Sun 3D Radiative Hydrodynamic Simulations
authors: Rimsha Hameed Syeda, Dustin Kempton, Viacheslav Sadykov, Irina Kitiashvili, Rafal Angryk
abstract: Numerical modeling of solar plasma dynamics is affected by the resolution of the computational grid. This often requires the estimation of subgrid processes related to the small-scale flow turbulence, as these processes play a critical role in momentum transport and energy dissipation. In this work, we investigate the use of deep learning techniques as surrogate models for subgrid turbulent transport in realistic hydrodynamic simulations of the quiet Sun. We describe the development of a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to capture spatial dependencies in 3D velocity fields, leveraging different activation functions, as well as different architectural designs. We specifically focus on the prediction of Reynolds stress tensor components. The resultant model integrates velocity vector components and scalar features, such as plasma density, to enhance prediction accuracy. We compare the 3DCNN model to other types of models, such as a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) and physics-based Gradient and Smagorinsky models, and show that the final model design reconstructs the Reynolds stress tensor components more accurately. Specifically, a 3DCNN model achieves an average improvement of ~31% on diagonal components and ~8% on the off-diagonal components of the stress tensor. Additionally, we show that applying a logarithmic data transformation of the target stress tensor components, to handle heavily skewed data, improves model performance. Results demonstrate the potential of deep learning, particularly CNNs, to approximate Reynolds stress tensor components for the upper solar convection zone and lower atmosphere, making them a viable candidate for modeling subgrid processes and a promising alternative to traditional turbulence models.

infographic.key_insight: A 3D CNN can learn subgrid turbulent transport in quiet-Sun simulations by using velocity and density fields to better reconstruct Reynolds stress tensor components than simpler ML or classic turbulence models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a data-driven surrogate for unresolved solar plasma turbulence, which could improve coarse-grid radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the solar convection zone and lower atmosphere.
method: Train a 3D convolutional neural network on 3D velocity fields plus scalar plasma density features.
Predict Reynolds stress tensor components and test activation/architecture variants, including a log transform of skewed targets.
Benchmark against an MLP and physics-based Gradient and Smagorinsky models.
infographic.evidence_signal: The final 3DCNN improved reconstruction by about 31% on diagonal stress components and about 8% on off-diagonal components relative to comparison baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the specific quiet-Sun simulation regime and careful handling of strongly skewed target distributions during training and deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Developing Machine Learning Models of Subgrid Turbulent Transport for Quiet Sun 3D Radiative Hydrodynamic Simulations

title: A Unified Gradient Theory for Frame-Indifferent Rates of Tensorial Internal Variables
authors: Luis Espath
abstract: We develop a thermodynamically consistent framework for weakly nonlocal continua with tensor-valued internal variables. Let $\boldsymbol{L}=\operatorname{grad}\boldsymbol{v}$, with stretching tensor $\boldsymbol{D}=\operatorname{sym}\boldsymbol{L}$ and spin tensor $\boldsymbol{W}=\operatorname{skw}\boldsymbol{L}$. We introduce the generators $\boldsymbolΓ_α=\boldsymbol{W}+α\boldsymbol{D}$, $α\in\{0,1\}$, which unify corotational and upper-convected transport. The resulting kinematic structure induces canonical frame-indifferent evolutions of both the internal variable and its spatial gradient, thereby providing a closure for gradient-dependent theories. Starting from the balances of linear momentum and microforces, together with an internal power expenditure depending on the internal variable and its gradient, we derive a local free-energy imbalance for incompressible isothermal processes. Under isotropy and inherited symmetry assumptions, this imbalance admits a canonical decomposition into contributions associated with $\boldsymbol{D}$, $\operatorname{grad}\boldsymbol{L}$, the generator-induced rate $\mathfrak{D}_α\boldsymbol{J}$, and its gradient $\mathfrak{D}^{\nabla}_α(\operatorname{grad}\boldsymbol{J})$. This decomposition yields explicit constitutive restrictions ensuring thermodynamic consistency and identifies the induced higher-order stress contributions arising from gradient dependence. Finally, we construct a coupled gradient theory combining viscoelasticity and constrained orientational order, in which distinct internal variables evolve under different transport mechanisms. The framework extends classical theories with tensorial internal variables, including Oldroyd-B and Landau-de Gennes-type models.

infographic.key_insight: A unified kinematic framework based on generator tensors [0mΓα [0mcombines corotational and upper-convected transport to produce frame-indifferent rates for tensor-valued internal variables and their gradients.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides thermodynamically consistent constitutive rules for gradient-dependent viscoelastic and orientational-order models, with direct relevance to advanced turbulence and complex-fluid simulations.
method: Define [0mL = grad v[0m, [0mD = sym L[0m, and [0mW = skw L[0m, then introduce [0mΓα = W + αD[0m to unify transport choices.
Derive a local free-energy imbalance from momentum balance, microforces, and internal power for incompressible isothermal processes.
Apply isotropy and symmetry assumptions to obtain constitutive restrictions and higher-order stress terms involving [0mD[0m, grad L, and generator-induced rates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a theoretical derivation and model construction; no numerical data, benchmarks, or experiments are reported.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is mathematically elegant but implementation will require careful treatment of higher-order gradients, objectivity, and boundary conditions in numerical solvers.
infographic.paper_title: A Unified Gradient Theory for Frame-Indifferent Rates of Tensorial Internal Variables

title: Energetics and Stochastics of Extreme Waves Breaking over a Symmetrical Breakwater
authors: Saulo Mendes, Yuchen He, Jérôme Kasparian, Amin Chabchoub
abstract: Rogue wave formation and enhancement over coastal areas have been documented over the last decade. This seems to contradict the observed low rogue wave (RW) probability near the surf zone. Without considering wave breaking, RW amplification is expected in this regime. To address this gap, we consider fully nonlinear effects of wave breaking through the proxy of height-to-depth ratio, spatial changes on the wavenumber through the WKB approximation, and slope-corrected refraction mild-slope equations on the energetics of irregular wave fields travelling over a breakwater. By increasing the significant wave height towards the breaking limit, the kinetic energy grows faster than the variance of the surface elevation due to nonlinearity. Thus, the kurtosis decays, albeit not to the point of getting sub-Gaussian statistics. We thereby resolve the apparent paradox of the occurrence probability of RW increase at the beginning of shoaling but subsequently decrease when wave breaking becomes dominant. Motivated by these theoretical developments, we experimentally probe inhomogeneous wave fields nearing the wave-breaking regime. We conduct unidirectional irregular wave experiments in a 30 m long wave flume, generating broad-banded waves over a symmetric submerged breakwater featuring a bottom slope of 1/5, allowing detailed characterization of spectral evolution and the persistence of elevated excess kurtosis even near the breaking limit for this steep slope. We thereby confirm that the excess kurtosis can still be large if the bottom slope is steep, and its maximum value is at least 4 times larger than in other ocean processes, occurring atop the breakwater and about half of its deep water peak wavelength distance after the shoal. As these conditions are typical near shorelines, this understanding is key to coastal areas.

infographic.key_insight: Wave breaking changes the usual shoaling-driven rogue-wave amplification: near a steep breakwater, nonlinearity first raises extreme-wave likelihood but then reduces it as breaking becomes dominant.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For coastal design and hazard assessment, steep-bottom geometry can sustain large excess kurtosis and elevated extreme-wave risk near the breakwater crest, so breaking effects must be included in nearshore predictions.
method: Model irregular waves over a submerged symmetric breakwater using fully nonlinear energetics.
Include wave-breaking effects via a height-to-depth proxy, WKB wavenumber variation, and slope-corrected mild-slope refraction.
Validate the theory with 30 m wave-flume experiments on broad-banded unidirectional waves over a 1/5 slope breakwater.
infographic.evidence_signal: The flume measurements show elevated excess kurtosis persists near the breaking limit and reaches a maximum at least four times larger than in other ocean processes, peaking over the breakwater and about half a deep-water wavelength shoreward of the shoal.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions are geometry- and slope-dependent, so results from the steep 1/5 breakwater may not transfer directly to milder coastal slopes or fully 2D sea states.
infographic.paper_title: Energetics and Stochastics of Extreme Waves Breaking over a Symmetrical Breakwater

title: Homothetic Self-Similar Solutions to the Incompressible Navier-Stokes Equations
authors: Tim Binz, Matei P. Coiculescu
abstract: We investigate homothetic forward self-similar solutions of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations: the solutions $\overline{U}$ for which both $\overline{U}$ and $β\overline{U}$ are self-similar profiles for some nontrivial $β$. Homothetic solutions are, in addition, the only solutions for which a singular limit argument can be used to prove non-uniqueness of Leray-Hopf solutions along the lines of the Jia-Šverák program. In three dimensions, and for sufficiently regular initial data, we prove a Liouville theorem that rules out the existence of non-trivial homothetic solutions. In two dimensions, our Liouville theorem proves that the only decaying homothetic solution is the Oseen vortex. In addition, we prove that the Euler operator linearized around the Oseen vortex is stable. On the other hand, we also discover a homothetic solution for which an unstable approximate eigenvalue of the linearized Euler operator exists.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that homothetic forward self-similar Navier–Stokes solutions are highly constrained: they do not exist nontrivially in 3D under regularity assumptions, and in 2D the only decaying case is the Oseen vortex.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This sharpens which self-similar flow structures are mathematically admissible, informing stability analysis, turbulence theory, and any singular-limit strategy for studying possible non-uniqueness in incompressible flows.
method: Prove a Liouville theorem for homothetic self-similar Navier–Stokes solutions.
Analyze the 2D decaying case and identify the Oseen vortex as the唯一 admissible solution.
Study the linearized Euler operator around the Oseen vortex to assess stability and detect an unstable approximate eigenvalue in a homothetic example.
infographic.evidence_signal: The results are theoretical and are supported by analytical proofs in 2D and 3D, including stability analysis of the linearized Euler operator and an example exhibiting an unstable approximate eigenvalue.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions apply to sufficiently regular initial data and decaying/self-similar settings, so they do not automatically rule out more singular or non-decaying flow scenarios.
infographic.paper_title: Homothetic Self-Similar Solutions to the Incompressible Navier-Stokes Equations

title: A Log-Gaussian Scale-Space Limiter for Hybrid Continuum--Ballistic Gas Dynamics
authors: Bjørn Wu
abstract: We propose a log-Gaussian scale-space limiter for hybrid continuum-ballistic gas dynamics. The method defines complementary continuum and ballistic weights as Gaussian cumulative probabilities in logarithmic Knudsen-number space. This construction gives a smooth numerical transition between Navier-Stokes-Fourier and kinetic/free-molecular fluxes and suppresses asymptotically invalid correction branches in the continuum and free-molecular limits. The limiter is incorporated into a conservative finite-volume interface flux by blending a Navier-Stokes-Fourier flux with a half-range Maxwellian kinetic flux. Numerical tests using one-dimensional DVM/BGK Fourier and Couette benchmarks show that rarefaction corrections improve macroscopic profiles relative to NSF. A parameter scan over the transition center and width gives a DVM/BGK-calibrated pair K0=0.03 and sigma=2.5, reducing the combined mean profile error by about 40% for the tested planar wall-bounded flows. The paper is intended as a proof-of-concept numerical method and calibration study.

infographic.key_insight: A log-Gaussian limiter smoothly blends continuum and ballistic gas fluxes in logarithmic Knudsen-number space to avoid using invalid asymptotic corrections in either regime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a practical hybrid flux model for rarefied gas simulations, improving wall-bounded flow predictions while preserving a conservative finite-volume formulation.
method: Defines continuum and ballistic weights as Gaussian CDFs in log(Kn) space.
Blends Navier-Stokes-Fourier flux with a half-range Maxwellian kinetic flux at interfaces.
Uses parameter calibration to select a transition center and width for planar benchmark flows.
infographic.evidence_signal: One-dimensional DVM/BGK Fourier and Couette benchmarks show improved macroscopic profiles and about a 40% reduction in combined mean profile error versus NSF for the tested cases.
infographic.watch_item: The calibration is benchmark-specific and proof-of-concept only, so transferability to more complex geometries or flow regimes still needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: A Log-Gaussian Scale-Space Limiter for Hybrid Continuum--Ballistic Gas Dynamics

title: Wall-scaled eddies and embedded shear layers in high-Reynolds-number moderate adverse-pressure-gradient boundary layers
authors: Ahmad Zarei, Mitchell Lozier, Ivan Marusic, Rahul Deshpande
abstract: This study compares high-Reynolds-number turbulent boundary layers under zero and low-to-moderate adverse pressure gradients, showing similar scaling and energy contributions from the wall-scaled attached-eddy hierarchy and superstructures in both flows. The main differences occur in the outer/wake region, where APG-induced energisation is linked to an outer-scaled, embedded-shear-layer-type organisation that progressively penetrates the logarithmic region as the pressure-gradient strength increases. The analysis uses two complementary datasets for ZPG and APG boundary layers at matched friction Reynolds numbers of approximately 10,000, with minimal upstream pressure-gradient history: a new two-point hot-wire dataset and a previously published two-dimensional particle image velocimetry dataset. In the hot-wire experiment, one probe is fixed near the wall while the second traverses the full boundary layer, allowing estimation of the linear coherence spectrum. The results confirm the geometric self-similarity of the wall-scaled eddy hierarchy that remains coherent with the wall. Using the linear coherence spectrum as a spectral filter shows that most of the additional APG-induced energy is incoherent with the wall and is linearly superimposed on the wall-coherent component of the streamwise variance. This wall-incoherent contribution explains the departure of the variance profile from the inverse logarithmic law observed in canonical high-Reynolds-number boundary layers. Conditional averaging of the particle image velocimetry data identifies the structures responsible for this energy amplification. The results link enhanced outer-region Reynolds stresses, an outer inflection point in the mean velocity profile, and an ejection-sweep organisation of Reynolds shear stress, all characteristic of shear-layer dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Moderate adverse pressure gradients leave the wall-scaled attached-eddy hierarchy largely unchanged, but add outer-region energy from an embedded shear-layer-like structure that becomes increasingly important toward the log layer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For high-Re boundary-layer design and modeling, pressure gradients mainly alter outer-region momentum transfer and variance through wall-incoherent energetic structures rather than by rewriting near-wall scaling.
method: Compared ZPG and APG boundary layers at matched friction Reynolds number near 10,000.
Used two-point hot-wire measurements to estimate the linear coherence spectrum and separate wall-coherent from wall-incoherent energy.
Used conditional averaging of PIV data to identify the structures associated with APG-induced energisation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two complementary datasets, the wall-coherent attached-eddy contribution remained similar, while the extra APG variance was largely incoherent with the wall and associated with outer shear-layer organization.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions are drawn for low-to-moderate APG cases with minimal upstream history, so stronger pressure gradients or different development histories may not follow the same scaling.
infographic.paper_title: Wall-scaled eddies and embedded shear layers in high-Reynolds-number moderate adverse-pressure-gradient boundary layers

title: Structure-preserving variational neural fields: Uncertainty-quantified reduced-order modeling of nonlinear conservation laws
authors: Aviral Prakash, Marc L. Klasky
abstract: Reduced-order models, such as latent dynamics models, are becoming mainstream for accelerating simulations for parameterized physical systems governed by nonlinear conservation laws. However, most existing latent dynamics frameworks suffer from two important limitations: they do not provide uncertainty estimates for model predictions, and they do not guarantee adherence to the underlying conservation laws. While these challenges have been addressed separately in prior work, a unified framework that simultaneously provides uncertainty quantification and exact conservation-law preservation remains largely unexplored. In this work, we develop a variational latent neural field framework that integrates Gaussian process-inspired surrogates, enabling estimation of predictive confidence for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution parameter regimes. Three variants of the framework are considered: IRS-UQ, PI-IRS-UQ, and ECLEIRS-UQ, corresponding to unconstrained, physics-informed, and conservation-structure-preserving formulations, respectively. Exact conservation-structure preservation is achieved by embedding the solution dynamics within a conservation-law manifold through a space-time divergence-free representation of the solution-flux field. We demonstrate the applicability of the framework through three numerical experiments: 1) 1-D advection, 2) 2-D Euler and 3) 2-D shallow water equations in parameterized settings. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach provides accurate predictions together with uncertainty estimates, while remaining robust to sparse and noisy training data. Comparisons between the proposed three approaches show that conservation-structure preserving latent representations improve robustness to degraded training data while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy and uncertainty quantification capability.

infographic.key_insight: A variational latent neural field can jointly predict reduced-order dynamics, quantify uncertainty, and exactly preserve conservation laws for nonlinear PDEs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a surrogate modeling path for CFD and multiphysics applications where fast parameter sweeps are needed but physics consistency and confidence estimates are essential.
method: Uses Gaussian process-inspired latent surrogates to estimate predictive uncertainty.
Compares three variants: IRS-UQ, PI-IRS-UQ, and ECLEIRS-UQ.
Enforces exact conservation via a space-time divergence-free solution-flux representation on a conservation-law manifold.
infographic.evidence_signal: The framework is evaluated on 1-D advection, 2-D Euler, and 2-D shallow water systems under parameterized settings, including sparse and noisy training data.
infographic.watch_item: The conservation-preserving formulation may be more complex to implement and train than unconstrained latent models, especially for high-dimensional CFD systems.
infographic.paper_title: Structure-preserving variational neural fields: Uncertainty-quantified reduced-order modeling of nonlinear conservation laws

title: Colloid recovery from porous structures under ambient flow: enhanced extraction via phoretic and osmotic mechanisms
authors: Jitendra Dhakar, Kapil Upadhyaya, Akash Choudhary
abstract: Chemical gradients are widely employed to enhance particle transport in porous media, such as laundry detergency and enhanced oil recovery. Diffusiophoresis and diffusioosmosis refer to the movement of colloid and movement of near-surface fluid in response to electrolyte gradients, respectively. These mechanisms play a crucial role in colloid and drug transport in constricted regions where bulk transport is infeasible. Our earlier work [Tiwari et al., Langmuir 41, 18583 (2025)] has shown that phoretic and osmotic transport in dead-end micro-pores can be controlled by orienting salt gradients into or out of the pores; however, the extent to which this orientation influences large-scale spatiotemporal patterns and colloid extraction is not thoroughly explored. In this work, we study the phoretic and osmotic colloidal extraction from porous structure exposed to an ambient flow. We characterize the impact of solute gradient orientation, such as solute-out (i.e., solute-emitting porous media) and solute-in (i.e., solute-consuming media) modes. The two-dimensional porous structure is made of a number of pillars/fibers arranged in a lattice ordered hexagonal packing with equal spacing. The results from finite-element simulations show that phoretic colloidal extraction exhibits a qualitatively distinct behavior in the two modes: in the solute-out mode, colloids are extracted from the peripheral region of the porous structure, whereas in the solute-in mode, extraction predominantly occurs from the stagnant core. Diffusioosmotic slip on the internal surface of pillars/fibres further amplifies extraction in both modes, with a relatively larger enhancement in the solute-in mode due to internal spatiotemporal flow patterns. Beyond demonstrating the sensitivity of osmotic transport in porous media, these insights can guide enhanced membrane filtration, laundry detergency, and enhanced oil recovery.

infographic.key_insight: Orienting the salt gradient changes where colloids are extracted from porous media: solute-out favors peripheral removal, while solute-in drives extraction from the stagnant core, and diffusioosmotic slip boosts both.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling phoretic and osmotic transport in porous structures could improve membrane filtration, laundry detergency, and enhanced oil recovery.
method: 2D porous medium modeled as hexagonally packed pillars/fibers with equal spacing
Finite-element simulations of colloid transport under ambient flow and electrolyte gradients
Compared solute-out (emitting) versus solute-in (consuming) gradient orientations with/without diffusioosmotic slip
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulation results show qualitatively distinct extraction patterns for the two gradient orientations, with diffusioosmotic slip further amplifying extraction and giving a larger gain in the solute-in case.
infographic.watch_item: The study is simulation-based, so real porous-media performance may depend on pore-scale geometry, chemistry, and flow conditions not fully captured here.
infographic.paper_title: Colloid recovery from porous structures under ambient flow: enhanced extraction via phoretic and osmotic mechanisms

title: Secondary Flows and Near-Wall Turbulence in Channel Flow with Longitudinal Ribs
authors: Ranjan Kushwaha, S. Sarkar, Gautam Biswas
abstract: This study employs the Large Eddy Simulation (LES) to investigate secondary flows and near-wall turbulence induced by two types of surface-mounted longitudinal ribs, namely rectangular and triangular, in a channel flow. The friction Reynolds number, based on friction velocity and channel height H, is set at 220. The rib aspect ratio W/h, where W and h represent the width and height of the rib, is 2, and the rib spacing, S is 0.6H. The results indicate formation of two counter-rotating vortices between the adjacent ribs for both the cases considered. The roughness function is higher with the rectangular rib as compared to that of the triangular rib. At the location of the mid-plane on the rectangular ribs, the wall shear stress is relatively lower as compared to that of the location of mid-plane between the ribs. Conversely, for the case of triangular rib, the opposite pattern is observed. Normal Reynolds stress exhibits strong anisotropic behaviour near the wall for both the cases, overlapping above 0.4H. Between 0.4H and 0.8H, the variation in normal Reynolds stresses is linear. Near the wall, higher production of turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) and normal Reynolds stresses are observed with the triangular rib as compared to those of the rectangular rib. The ratio of production to dissipation is unity in the log-law region.

infographic.key_insight: Longitudinal ribs generate counter-rotating secondary vortices and strongly alter near-wall turbulence, with rectangular ribs producing a larger roughness effect while triangular ribs intensify near-wall TKE production.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Rib shape and spacing can be tuned to control drag, wall shear, and mixing in channel flows, which is useful for heat-transfer surfaces and roughness design.
method: Large Eddy Simulation (LES) of channel flow at friction Reynolds number 220.
Compared rectangular and triangular surface-mounted longitudinal ribs with aspect ratio W/h = 2 and spacing S = 0.6H.
Analyzed secondary vortices, wall shear stress, Reynolds stresses, and turbulence production/dissipation across the wall-normal direction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports two counter-rotating vortices between adjacent ribs in both cases, a higher roughness function for rectangular ribs, and distinct wall-shear-stress and Reynolds-stress profiles.
infographic.watch_item: Results are from a single Reynolds number and a specific rib geometry, so broader design conclusions may require additional parameter sweeps and validation.
infographic.paper_title: Secondary Flows and Near-Wall Turbulence in Channel Flow with Longitudinal Ribs
